question:
Patient note:
A 53-year-old woman presented to the rheumatology-pulmonary shared clinic for routine follow-up and comprehensive assessment before her upcoming work-related travel. She was diagnosed with seropositive rheumatoid arthritis at age 38 after several months of symmetric pain and morning stiffness in the metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints; radiographs at that time already showed marginal erosions of the second and third MCPs, and she has since been managed with methotrexate 20 mg weekly, hydroxychloroquine 200 mg twice daily, and a low-dose prednisone taper during flares, with good control of disease activity and no extra-articular nodulosis, vasculitis, or scleritis. She independently performs all instrumental activities of daily living, balances her household finances, and continues in her position as an administrative analyst without lapses in memory or executive function. About nine years ago she began experiencing progressive exertional dyspnea and wheeze that was initially labeled “adult-onset asthma,” but spirometry obtained three months ago demonstrated an FEV1/FVC ratio of 61 % with a post-bronchodilator increase of only 5 %, consistent with fixed airflow limitation; high-resolution CT of the chest showed centrilobular emphysematous changes predominantly in the upper lobes. She now uses tiotropium 18 µg inhaled every morning, fluticasone-salmeterol 250/50 µg twice daily, and albuterol as needed, averaging two rescue puffs per week; she has never required invasive ventilation, and her last hospital admission for an acute exacerbation was five years ago during a viral upper-respiratory illness. She smoked one pack of cigarettes daily from age 17 to 47 and quit when the pulmonary diagnosis was explained; she has not resumed tobacco use and drinks wine socially, no more than one glass on weekends. Type 2 diabetes mellitus was identified at age 48 during routine screening when her fasting plasma glucose measured 138 mg/dL; lifestyle modification plus metformin 1000 mg twice daily have maintained her most recent hemoglobin A1c at 6.7 %. She denies visual blurring, paresthesias of the feet, episodes of hypoglycemia, proteinuria on prior laboratory work, or any hospitalizations for ketoacidosis or hyperosmolar crises. Serum creatinine has remained between 0.8 and 0.9 mg/dL, and estimated glomerular filtration rate last month was 92 mL/min/1.73 m² with a urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio below 20 mg/g. She has never experienced crushing chest pressure, diaphoresis with exertion, syncope, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, or ankle swelling, and an echocardiogram performed two years ago for a systolic murmur revealed normal left-ventricular size and ejection fraction of 62 %, trivial tricuspid regurgitation, and no regional wall-motion abnormalities. She routinely walks two flights of stairs without calf pain or rest symptoms, has no non-healing skin lesions, and pulses in the femoral, posterior tibial, and dorsalis pedis arteries have been documented as symmetric and full. There is no prior history of transient unilateral weakness, aphasia, facial droop, seizures, or visual field cuts, and neurologic examination last visit showed intact strength, sensation, and coordination; she writes and types without difficulty, and there is no past imaging suggestive of cerebral infarction. She has never required upper endoscopy, denies dyspepsia, hematemesis, melena, or occult blood on fecal immunochemical tests, and abdominal ultrasound obtained incidentally during a research study displayed a smooth hepatic contour with normal parenchymal echotexture; liver transaminases, bilirubin, and international normalized ratio have always been within reference ranges. She is HIV-negative on routine occupational screening, has no personal or family history of lymphoid or myeloid malignancy, and dermatologic review is negative for B-symptom-associated night sweats or unintentional weight loss. Current medications in addition to those noted include low-dose aspirin 81 mg daily for primary cardiovascular prevention, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, folic acid 1 mg daily to mitigate methotrexate toxicity, and calcium-vitamin D supplementation because of chronic glucocorticoid use during arthritis flares. Vital signs in clinic read: temperature 36.7 °C, blood pressure 128/74 mm Hg in the right arm seated, heart rate 76 beats per minute regular, respiratory rate 15 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 95 % on ambient air, dropping to 92 % after a brisk 100-meter corridor walk. Physical examination shows an alert, well-nourished woman in no acute distress; cardiac auscultation reveals a soft midsystolic murmur at the left upper sternal border without radiation, lungs demonstrate scattered end-expiratory wheezes but no crackles, the abdomen is soft with no organomegaly, and there is mild fusiform swelling of the second and third MCPs with minimal tenderness but no tophi or active synovitis elsewhere. There are no peripheral edemas, distal pulses are 2+ throughout, and capillary refill is under two seconds. Laboratory studies drawn this morning reveal hemoglobin 12.6 g/dL, white blood cell count 6.1 × 10⁹/L, platelets 245 × 10⁹/L, sodium 139 mmol/L, potassium 4.1 mmol/L, bicarbonate 24 mmol/L, BUN 14 mg/dL, creatinine 0.9 mg/dL, AST 22 U/L, ALT 25 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 68 U/L, total bilirubin 0.7 mg/dL, fasting glucose 124 mg/dL, and an LDL cholesterol of 78 mg/dL. Hand radiographs ordered today for surveillance will be reviewed at her next appointment.

Question: What is the patient's Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI)? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The age-adjusted Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI) adds age points to the weights of qualifying diagnoses present at assessment.
- Age 53 (50–59 years): +1.
- Rheumatic disease: seropositive erosive rheumatoid arthritis → +1.
- Chronic pulmonary disease: fixed airflow obstruction and CT-confirmed emphysema → +1.
- Diabetes without end-organ damage: metformin-treated type 2 diabetes without documented nephropathy, neuropathy, or retinopathy → +1.
- Other CCI conditions: no reported myocardial infarction, heart failure, peripheral vascular or cerebrovascular disease, dementia, hemiplegia, ulcer disease, liver disease, moderate-to-severe renal disease, malignancy, or AIDS → 0.
Total = 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 0 = 4.
Final answer: 4
